grammarSources.title: A Grammar of the Kashmiri Language, as spoken in the valley of Kashmir, North India
grammarSources.creator: Rev. T. R. Wade, B.D., M.R.A.S.; with an introduction by Dr. Robert Cust
grammarSources.publisher: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, London
grammarSources.license: Public domain. Published 1888; the archive.org metadata records a copyright expiry date of 1888 and states no licence or rights restriction.
grammarSources.textLayer: The OCR text layer is 100% Latin romanization and contains zero Arabic-script characters, so this is a grammar and paradigm reference, not a Perso-Arabic reading source. It is therefore deliberately NOT part of readingLibrary. Unlike the Nastaliq scans, its text layer is clean and readable.
grammarSources.scope: Describes spoken Kashmiri of 1888 in the author's own romanization. The preface states there was then no written authority for spelling, so forms are phonetic. Use it for STRUCTURE (case, alignment, paradigms) and cross-check actual spellings against the modern corpus and dictionary, not the reverse.

rulesUsed.rule: Ergative/agentive alignment in the past transitive
rulesUsed.quote: The nominative case is used with intransitive verbs in all tenses, and with transitive verbs in the present, future, and past imperfect tenses.
rulesUsed.note: Past perfect transitive is therefore NOT nominative: "Meh mor haput" I killed a he-bear, "Meh mari hapata" I killed she-bears. The agentive Meh is the modern مےٚ (contrast nominative بہٕ).

rulesUsed.rule: The past transitive verb agrees with the OBJECT
rulesUsed.quote: After the past tense (not imperfect) of a transitive verb the accusative always agrees with the verb in number and gender.
rulesUsed.note: Object agreement, not subject agreement, is why choosing a generic first-person ending produces an agreement error.

rulesUsed.rule: "have" is expressed as "to be" + a dative
rulesUsed.quote: The verb "to be," with the dative pronominal affixes, is constantly used to denote possession, meaning "I have," etc.
rulesUsed.note: chhum = is to me = I have him; chhem = she is to me = I have her. So "every person shall have" is a dative possessor plus the copula, not a verb meaning "obtain".

rulesUsed.rule: The genitive agrees with the POSSESSED noun
rulesUsed.quote: The genitive affixes, -sund, -hund, -uk, -un, and -ur, are all inflected and agree with the noun possessed in number and gender.
rulesUsed.note: A feminine possessed noun therefore takes the feminine genitive, e.g. سُنٛد (m) beside سٕنٛز (f).

rulesUsed.rule: The copula follows the subject; the complement stays nominative
rulesUsed.quote: Nar chhu garni. Fire is hot. / Suh chhu mahnius. He is a man.
rulesUsed.note: Subject then copula then predicate, matching the modern corpus template سٲری اِنسان چھِ آزاد زامٕتؠ.

rulesUsed.quote: There are no words in the Kashmiri language exactly answering to the articles "a," "an," and "the."
rulesUsed.note: The bare noun covers both; akh (one) or kanh (some) may be added but are not required.

rulesUsed.rule: Genitive and adjective precede the noun they modify
rulesUsed.quote: A noun in the genitive case usually precedes its governing noun, and an adjective the substantive that it qualifies.

rulesUsed.rule: The past copula inflects for gender
rulesUsed.quote: Past indefinite: Su os (he was) beside osa (she was / they were).
rulesUsed.note: This is the open question for the modern form: the masculine is اوس (258 corpus hits); the feminine spelling in current text is not settled. Do not silently pick one.
